summary.text: The brain is an organ made of nervous tissue that serves as the center of the nervous system in all vertebrates and most invertebrates.
It receives information from the sensory nervous system, processes it, and coordinates muscle activity and the endocrine system.
Together, the brain and spinal cord make up the central nervous system in all vertebrates.

facts.label: Links per neuron
facts.value: Synapses connect each neuron to several thousand others

facts.label: Signal speed
facts.value: Action potentials travel 1 to 100 meters per second

items.prompt: Your hand jerks away from a hot stove before you consciously decide to move. What can handle basic responses like this without the brain?

options.label: Only the cerebral cortex
Only the prefrontal cortex
Glial cells working alone
The spinal cord or peripheral ganglia

items.explain: Basic responses such as reflexes can be mediated by the spinal cord or peripheral ganglia, though sophisticated, purposeful control needs the centralized brain.

items.prompt: Besides neurons, the brain is full of glial cells. Which job do glial cells do?

options.label: Fire bursts of action potentials
Release neurotransmitter at synapses
Send signals along long axons
Insulate and support the neurons

items.explain: Glial cells perform critical functions including structural support, metabolic support, insulation and guidance of development.

items.prompt: Neurons and glial cells make up the brain. Why are neurons considered special among them?

options.label: They can send signals to specific target cells, sometimes far away
They hold the brain together as structural support
They insulate and protect the other cells
They are the only cells that need energy

items.explain: The property that makes neurons unique is their ability to send signals to specific target cells, sometimes over long distances.

items.prompt: An action potential traveling along an axon arrives at a synapse. What does its arrival cause to be released?

options.label: Myelin
A neurotransmitter
A new glial cell
A fixative

items.explain: The arrival of an action potential at a synapse causes a neurotransmitter to be released, and it binds to receptor molecules in the target cell's membrane.

items.prompt: Biologists compare how invertebrate and vertebrate brains arise. What differs?

options.label: Vertebrate brains come from segmental ganglia, each serving one segment
Both come from identical enlargements of a neural tube
Invertebrate brains come from segmental ganglia, each serving one segment
Invertebrate brains grow from the midline and control every segment

items.explain: Invertebrate brains arise from paired segmental ganglia, each responsible only for its own body segment, while vertebrate brains develop from the midline with centralized control over all segments.

items.prompt: Modern neuroscience models treat the brain as a biological computer, quite different from a digital one. In what way are the two alike?

options.label: Both run on the same mechanism
Both take in information, store it and process it
Both keep memory apart from processing
Both work only with on and off signals

items.explain: The brain is treated as very different in mechanism from a digital computer, but similar in that it acquires information from the world, stores it and processes it in a variety of ways.

paragraphs.heading: The control centre
paragraphs.text: The brain is the organ at the centre of the nervous system in all vertebrates and in most invertebrates. It is built from nervous tissue and usually sits in the head, close to the organs for senses like sight, hearing and smell. It takes in information from the senses, works on it through thought and reasoning, and coordinates muscle activity and the endocrine system. Together with the spinal cord, it makes up the central nervous system of every vertebrate.

paragraphs.heading: Why a central brain helps
paragraphs.text: Brains steer the body's other organs from one central place. They do it in two ways: by producing patterns of muscle activity, and by triggering the release of chemicals called hormones. This central control lets an animal react to changes around it quickly and in a coordinated way. Simple responses such as reflexes can be handled by the spinal cord, but purposeful behaviour based on complex input needs a brain to pull the information together.

paragraphs.heading: Three basic parts
paragraphs.text: Every vertebrate brain can be divided, as it forms in the embryo, into three parts: the forebrain, the midbrain and the hindbrain. The spinal cord, which directly handles body functions below the head, can be seen as a tail-end continuation of the hindbrain, enclosed in the backbone. Inside, the brain shows darker regions called grey matter separated by lighter regions called white matter.

paragraphs.heading: Neurons and glia
paragraphs.text: Brains of every species are made mainly of two classes of cell, neurons and glial cells. Glia come in several types and give structural and metabolic support, insulation, and guidance as the brain develops. Neurons are usually seen as the most important. The human cerebral cortex holds roughly 14 to 16 billion of them, and the cerebellum an estimated 55 to 70 billion, each linked to several thousand others.

paragraphs.heading: How signals travel
paragraphs.text: What makes neurons special is that they can send signals to particular target cells, sometimes far away. They do this through an axon, a thin fibre that grows out from the cell body and branches to reach other areas. Signals run along it as action potentials, electrochemical pulses lasting under a thousandth of a second and moving at 1 to 100 metres per second. At a synapse, a specialised junction, the arriving pulse makes the cell release a chemical called a neurotransmitter, which binds to receptors on the target cell.

paragraphs.heading: A very long reach
paragraphs.text: Axons can be startlingly long. Picture a pyramidal cell from the cerebral cortex blown up until its cell body is the size of a person. Its axon, scaled up the same way, would become a cable a few centimetres thick running for more than a kilometre.

paragraphs.heading: Still an open puzzle
paragraphs.text: Scientists now understand in great detail how single brain cells work. How millions of them cooperate is still unsolved. Some recent models describe the brain as a biological computer: built very differently from a digital one, but alike in that it gathers information from the world, stores it and processes it.
